clue.text: Out of true, like site for observatory

parts.note: as means like, in the sense 'as a lion' for 'like a lion'
Kew, in west London, was home to the Kew Observatory (the King's Observatory)

explanation.surface: Something is crooked, rather like the location chosen for a telescope.
explanation.walkthrough: KEW is a London district, best known for its botanical gardens; it also had a famous observatory.
explanation.definitionFit: Something crooked or skewed is not aligned straight, which is what being out of true means.

clue.text: Old Harry lost a month's start, if up before the finish

indicators.note: lost together with start means the month's opening letter goes missing
start points at the very first letter as the one to be dropped

parts.note: March is a month

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word if is written upwards, read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
the end means the finish

explanation.surface: Someone called Harry lost the start of a month's holiday, if only he'd come up before the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost ... start' drops the M from MARCH; 'up' reverses IF to FI. Old Harry, Old Nick and Old Scratch are old nicknames for the Devil.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Harry is a traditional nickname for Satan, the chief demon.

clue.text: Ring given by monarch to mistress?

parts.note: K is the abbreviation for king, a monarch
Nell Gwyn was the famous mistress of King Charles II

explanation.surface: A ring a king gives his lover, a picture of royal romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' looks like a jewel; it is the sound of a bell tolled for a death.
explanation.definitionFit: The slow tolling of a bell, especially at a funeral, is its ring.

clue.text: By which means West enclosed the sum needed less a pound

parts.note: herewith is the letter-writer's word for enclosed with this

explanation.surface: Asking how the West contained a sum short of a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: A second route: WHEREWITHAL, the sum needed, less A L (a pound) gives the answer too. Both wordplays lead to the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: This old-fashioned word means with which, the means used to do something.

clue.text: Yellow grain is product of Wales, some may say

definitions.text: product of Wales, some may say
definitions.note: said aloud, Wales sounds like whales, the sperm whale being where this waxy substance comes from

parts.note: amber is a yellowish-orange colour
gr is the standard abbreviation for grain, the tiny unit of weight
taken as written

explanation.surface: A yellow cereal crop is said to be something made in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on sound: 'some may say' tells you to hear Wales as whales. The waxy substance forms in the gut of sperm whales and was prized in perfume.
explanation.definitionFit: This waxy substance is produced in the intestines of sperm whales, so it is a whale product.

clue.text: Gin said to make fortune for this Chinese youth

definitions.text: Gin said to make fortune for this Chinese youth

parts.words: Gin said to make fortune for this Chinese youth
parts.note: 'gin' heard as djinn: a genie of a lamp made the fortune of the poor boy in the Arabian Nights tale, set in China

explanation.surface: A drink is supposed to have made one young Chinese man rich.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Arabian Nights story the poor boy lives in China and the genie (djinn) of the lamp makes him rich; 'Gin' sounds like djinn.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the poor youth of the pantomime tale whose genie brings him riches and a princess.

clue.text: Rabbit about poor lad's mishap

indicators.note: about means the rabbit's word goes round, enclosing the other letters

parts.note: a buck is a male rabbit

indicators.note: poor suggests the word is in a bad state, its letters jumbled

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A rabbit circling a poor boy's accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges LAD to ADL; 'about' puts BUCK round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Misfortune is a synonym, as a mishap is an unlucky event.

clue.text: Send back transfer

definitions.meaning: refer back, as a higher court sends a case to a lower one
send money by post or bank, as in paying a bill

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both referring a case back for decision and sending payment.

clue.text: Plan for Lady Smith's link-up?

parts.note: a plan (map) for the relief of Ladysmith, the besieged town in the Boer War, read as Lady Smith

explanation.surface: Arrangements for a woman named Smith to be joined to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Ladysmith in South Africa was besieged in the Boer War; its relief in 1900 was celebrated. A map showing hills in raised form carries this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A map showing land height in raised form, read cryptically as a chart for lifting a siege.

clue.text: Mathematical functions without point

parts.note: sine is Latin for without, as in sine qua non
S, south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Equations that lack a decimal point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like an instruction to remove something; it is the Latin word.
explanation.definitionFit: Trigonometric ratios such as these are examples of mathematical functions.

clue.text: County town of Ohio?

definitions.meaning: an English county created in 1974 and abolished in 1996, around Middlesbrough
a large city on Lake Erie in the US state of Ohio

explanation.surface: A request to name a county town, here oddly placed in Ohio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'County town' is a British phrase for the administrative centre of a county, so the clue invites one reading while splitting it into two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: The same name served both a former county in north-east England and the major Ohio city on Lake Erie.

clue.text: Prospero's city entitlement

definitions.meaning: in Shakespeare's The Tempest, Prospero is the deposed duke of this Italian city
read as en-title-ment: the city gives Prospero his title, Duke of the place

explanation.surface: Asking which city a magician in a play has a claim to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entitlement' is used playfully: the city is Prospero's title, as Duke of the city, rather than a right he is owed.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero, Shakespeare's magician, was the rightful Duke of this Lombard city, so it is both his city and his title.

clue.text: Fleas teased? Not true

indicators.note: teased means combed out or pulled apart, as fibres are, so these letters are worked into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone has been making fun of fleas, and the claim is untrue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'teased' rearranges the letters of FLEAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Untrue and wrong are synonyms of this word.

clue.text: Thomas wasn't, surely!

definitions.meaning: the apostle Thomas doubted the Resurrection, so he was not without doubt

explanation.surface: An exclamation that Thomas cannot have done something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubting Thomas' is the apostle who would not believe until he saw the wounds; the cryptic half reads the answer as 'free of doubt', which Thomas was not.
explanation.definitionFit: Certainly and undoubtedly are synonyms, both meaning without question.

clue.text: Samuel's teacher goes to Jerusalem, taking away letters

parts.note: in the Bible, the boy Samuel was raised and taught by the priest Eli
Sion (Zion) is a biblical name for Jerusalem

explanation.surface: A biblical teacher travels to Jerusalem and removes the post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes to' just joins the pieces. 'Letters' looks like post being taken away; it means letters of the alphabet, as in dropping sounds in speech.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the omission of sounds or letters in speech or writing, as in 'don't' for 'do not'.

clue.text: Rally is in trouble with Orsino's people

definitions.note: plural: Orsino is Duke of Illyria in Twelfth Night, so his subjects

indicators.note: in trouble suggests the words Rally is in are in disorder, their letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A rally is in difficulty with a duke's subjects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' rearranges RALLY IS IN. 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Orsino rules the Adriatic land of Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, so his subjects are its inhabitants.

clue.text: Relation finds reference to Mozart's work in text returned with article

parts.note: K stands for Köchel, whose catalogue numbers identify Mozart's works
taken as written

indicators.note: returned means the word for a text is read backwards

parts.note: MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a written text
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A relative is located from a Mozart catalogue number inside a returned script with an item attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns MS round to SM. K numbers (after Ludwig von Köchel) are the standard way to cite Mozart's pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A family member or blood relative is a synonym.

clue.text: Going round island has no new order for toys

indicators.note: new order says the words has no take another arrangement of their letters
going round means the island's letters rotate, the first moving to the end

parts.note: Sark is one of the Channel Islands

explanation.surface: Travelling round an island that lacks a new system for toys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new order' rearranges HAS NO; 'Going round' moves the S of SARK to the end to make ARKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooden toy boats with pairs of animals were classic nursery playthings.

clue.text: Hence southern views all round

parts.note: from this point every direction you look is south

explanation.surface: From here there is a southward panorama on every side.
explanation.walkthrough: At the top of the globe, every direction is south.
explanation.definitionFit: At the Earth's northernmost point, all directions lead southward.

clue.text: Ambiguous sort of help, detectives in their turn receive

indicators.note: receive means the detectives' letters take in the other piece, holding it inside
in their turn means the detectives' letters are turned round, read backwards

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the detective branch of British police

indicators.note: sort of suggests a version of the word help, its letters arranged differently

explanation.surface: A vague kind of assistance, which detectives take in when it is their go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in their turn' reverses CID to DIC; 'sort of' rearranges HELP to ELPH; 'receive' puts ELPH inside DIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Like the Delphic oracle's riddling pronouncements, something obscure that can be read more than one way.

clue.text: Assemble for prayer

definitions.meaning: a short prayer for a particular day in the church calendar

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to gather, and the noun is a short liturgical prayer of the day.

clue.text: What a little duck she is!

definitions.text: What a little duck she is!

parts.words: What a little duck she is!
parts.note: a young duck not yet able to fly is so called, and 'duck' is also a term of endearment for a lively young woman, as in 1920s slang

explanation.surface: An admiring remark about a sweet young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Two readings: a young wild duck is called this, and so was a fashionable, carefree young woman of the 1920s.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a fledgling duck and a bob-haired, jazz-age young woman.

clue.text: He held up infantry on guard

parts.note: foot soldiers are the infantry, as in 'regiment of foot'
a pad is protective guard, as a cricketer's leg pad

explanation.surface: A soldier delayed foot troops on sentry duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held up' looks like delayed; it means robbed, as a highwayman does.
explanation.definitionFit: A robber on foot who waylaid travellers, the walking version of a highwayman.

clue.text: There's daily competition for ministerial office

definitions.meaning: the name of a numbers game run in newspapers, including The Times
a government minister's area of responsibility, such as a department

explanation.surface: A remark that newspapers run contests for government posts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daily' here means a daily newspaper, which ran a prize game of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a newspaper prize game and the set of duties a government minister holds.

clue.text: Pretended to be puzzled

definitions.meaning: acted a part, put on a show
as a verb, set a problem, as a question set for someone

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both feigned and presented a problem, as one sets a question.

clue.text: American pioneer expressman-born on Thursday?

definitions.meaning: William ... co-founded the Wells ... express company
the rhyme says 'Thursday's child has far to go'

explanation.surface: An American pioneer of express delivery, perhaps born on a Thursday.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'Monday's child' says Thursday's child 'has far to go'.
explanation.definitionFit: William Fargo was a founder of the Wells Fargo and American Express companies.

clue.text: Second TV series is a hit

parts.note: M*A*S*H was the long-running American TV comedy set in a Korean War field hospital

explanation.surface: A follow-up television show turns out to be a success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like 'follow-up'; it is just S.
explanation.definitionFit: A big success, like a box-office triumph, is a synonym.

clue.text: Bearded warden has no right to be disorderly

indicators.note: to be disorderly says the letters left are scrambled out of order

explanation.surface: A bearded prison officer misbehaves without permission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has no right' takes R from WARDEN, leaving WADEN, which 'to be disorderly' rearranges. 'Bearded' is botanical: having bristles, as barley does.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany, grasses with bristly tips such as barley are described with this word.

clue.text: Earldom where poet on the way up met an absentee

definitions.meaning: a Scottish earldom, held by the Dalrymple family

definitions.text: where poet on the way up met an absentee
definitions.meaning: from the rhyme 'As I was going up the ... / I met a man who wasn't there'

explanation.surface: A noble title, and a spot where a poet climbing met someone not present.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half quotes Hughes Mearns's poem 'Antigonish': 'As I was going up the stair / I met a man who wasn't there'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earl of the name is a Scottish peer, and the rhyme's speaker met the absent man on a step going up.

clue.text: Tongue of a serpent destroyed love

indicators.note: destroyed means the words a serpent are broken up and rebuilt in another order

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A snake's forked tongue ruined a romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' rearranges A SERPENT to ESPERANT. 'Tongue' looks like a snake's organ; it means a language.
explanation.definitionFit: This invented international language is a tongue in the sense of a language.

clue.text: Gambolled with. Diana's unwanted backing

parts.note: DI is a short form of Diana, plus the S of the possessive

indicators.note: backing means the word for unwanted is read backwards, from the end

parts.note: de trop is French, used in English, for unwanted or superfluous

explanation.surface: Someone played about with a woman's surplus support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns DE TROP round to PORTED. 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To frolic or romp playfully is a synonym, as children play in a field.

clue.text: See about director-general for plant

indicators.note: about means the word see goes round, enclosing the other letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to ask a top boss about a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a factory; it is the grassy marsh plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A grass-like plant of wet ground is an example of a plant.
